blocks.h: FIFTY-ONE MINUTES IN FULL SUN
Roya Publication No. 121
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Fifty-one minutes is the length of a telephone call. A man took it on a summer morning twenty-six years ago, standing beside a road in full sun, and he has kept the record of it ever since. He can tell you the number. He cannot tell you why he kept it.

Rostam Bina makes one medicine. Forty million Americans take it every Thursday with a glass of water, and so does he. His company is worth more than every airline in the country, and most of that worth sits in the retirement funds of teachers and nurses. For twenty years the magazines have called him the calm man. People did not put their savings in a tablet. They put them in him.

Then a newspaper prints a photograph of Rostam at the door of a house on the coast, with a woman who is not his wife. Ninety billion dollars are gone in a morning. The board wants an apology on film. Thirty-five takes in a studio have all come out the same: smooth, correct, and sorry about nothing.

So the crew is sent home. One camera operator comes to his house instead, and she has one condition. There will be no script. Every Thursday he will sit down and say what he did, from the beginning, in his own words.
He agrees. It seems efficient.
He has a great deal to say. She has not told him why she asked for the job.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book began with one question. What if we did not feel remorse for our past mistakes?

I do not mean forgetting them. I mean remembering every one of them clearly and feeling nothing when we do. I wondered what kind of person that would make. Part of me thought it might make a stronger one. A person like that could take risks without flinching. He could fail in public on Monday and begin again on Tuesday. He could chase one goal for thirty years and never lose a night’s sleep over something he did on the way. Much of what we call drive, and some of what we call creativity, may be only this: a lighter load.

Then I asked the second question. Would that person ever learn anything? We like to think we avoid a wrong act because we know it is wrong. I am no longer sure of that. We may avoid it because we remember how the last one felt.

The story came to me in a single week. Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, said publicly that he had been unfaithful to his wife. His board opened an investigation into reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Within days he had resigned from the company he built. As I write, that investigation has not reported, and I know no more than anyone else does.

What stayed with me was not the man. It was the speed. For years he had been one of the most admired builders alive, and people had put more than their money in him. It took less than a week. I watched it and thought that we should stop putting human beings on podiums. We never see their ordinary days. We do not know what they want when nobody is looking, or what they carry.

Nothing in this book is about him. Rostam Bina is invented. So are his company, his family, the town of Tres Olmos and every person in it. No medicine like his exists. Researchers have studied whether the pain of a memory can be dulled while the memory itself is kept. That work is real and it is careful. The tablet in this book is neither.
This is a dark book. It tells of harm to children, a suicide, and violence against a woman, and it tells them plainly.
I do not know the answer to my question. I only know which answer I am hoping for.
Chew Z
TAKE 36

It is Thursday. I take one tablet on Thursdays, with water. Forty million Americans do the same. I have done it for twenty-six years. She waits until the glass is empty. She takes the glass. She goes behind the camera.

The room is the long room at the back of my house. It has a redwood floor and a wall of glass that looks down a canyon, and the operator has hung a grey cloth over the glass so that the light will not change while I talk. There is one chair, one table, and one light on a stand. The camera sits on three legs. A red lamp on its front shows when it is recording. It is recording.
My name is Rostam Bina [ROS-tam bee-NAA]. In America I am called Ross. I am sixty-three. This is the thirty-sixth time I have made this statement.

The first thirty-five were made in the company’s studio in South San Francisco. It is a room with no windows and a carpet the colour of oatmeal. There was a crew of nine. A young woman from the communications office stood beside the camera and held up white cards with my words on them, and between takes another woman pressed powder onto my forehead with a small sponge.

After the thirty-fifth, the chairman of the board came down to watch the recordings with me. He is a heavy, tired man who used to run an airline. He watched four of them. Then he put his hand over his eyes.
“Ross,” he said. “Do you know what you look like?”
I said I looked like myself.

“You look like a man reading the weather. Rain on Tuesday. I regret the pain I have caused. Clearing by the weekend.” He took his hand away. “People have lost money. They want to see that it cost you something.”
I told him I had read the cards exactly as they were written.
“I know you did,” he said. “That’s the trouble.”

The crew was sent home. The operator asked for the job and I gave it to her. She came with one camera and one condition, which she had put in her letter. There would be no cards. Each Thursday I sit down and say what I did, from the beginning, in my own words. She films it. When there is one the board can use, we stop.
I agreed. It is efficient.
Item one.

For thirteen months I had sexual relations with a woman who is not my wife. The woman’s name is Helen. I have been married for thirty-four years. My wife lives in Oregon. We speak on the telephone on the first Sunday of each month. We have never divorced. The public found that reassuring, so neither of us corrected it.
The size of this depends on what I am. I will state it.

I make one medicine. The company makes it. I started the company. Forty million people in this country take the medicine once a week. That is one adult in six. There are more abroad. The company is worth more than every airline in America put together. Most of that worth is held in retirement funds, by teachers and bus drivers and nurses. When the story about Helen appeared, the share price fell eleven per cent in one morning. That is ninety billion dollars. A teacher in Fresno lost four thousand of them before she got out of bed.

That is why there is a camera. Men do what I did every day and nobody films them. For twenty years the magazines have called me the calm man. The calm man eats the same lunch every day. He has had the same wife for thirty-four years. He has never raised his voice in a meeting. People do not put their retirement in a medicine. They put it in a man.
There is an earring in my car. I will come to it.

Helen was the first person the company ever paid. The company was then one rented unit behind a tyre shop in South San Francisco. It had a roll-up metal door, a concrete floor that sweated in winter, and a second-hand refrigerator with a padlock on it. There was my brother, and there was me. Helen came in answer to a card we had pinned up at the college. She was twenty-four. Her hands were red from the cold in that unit, and she hummed under her breath while she worked. On her first day she washed every piece of glass we owned. Then she asked my brother why our notebooks were a disgrace.

She stayed twenty-five years. She kept the notebooks. She did not marry. She does not take the medicine. She does not take any medicine. I once watched her sit through a migraine, which is a headache bad enough to blind you, at her desk with a wet cloth over her eyes. It lasted three hours. There was aspirin in the drawer by her knee.
I asked her why she did not take it.
She said, from under the cloth, “Because then I wouldn’t know when it stopped.”
I recorded that as a quirk.

It began on a Wednesday in February of last year. We were working late on the annual filing, which is the long report a company must send the government every year. It was past eleven. The building was empty and the cleaners had been through, so the whole floor smelled of the pink soap they use, and it was raining hard against the windows. Helen had taken her shoes off under the table. She did that when she was tired. There were cartons of cold noodles between us.
She had been looking at the same page for some time. Then she put down her pencil.
“Twenty-four years,” she said. “Did you know that? Twenty-four years in March.”
I said I knew.
“Ross. In twenty-four years, have you ever once asked me a question that wasn’t about work?”
I thought about it. I told her that I had asked after her mother, in the spring her mother died.
“You asked what day the funeral was. So you could move a meeting.”
That was accurate. I said so.
She looked at me for a while. Then she put her hand flat on the table beside mine. She did not touch me. She left it there, an inch away, and I could feel that it was warm.
I will be accurate about why it began. I was not unhappy. I was not lonely. I do not get lonely. She was in the room. She had been in the room for twenty-four years.
The lawyers would like me to say that she started it. She put her hand on a table. I did the rest.

After that it was alternate Wednesdays, at a house I own on the coast near Pescadero. I should describe the house, because most of this item happened there. It stands by itself at the end of a dirt road, on a bluff above the ocean, with artichoke fields behind it. It is made of grey wood and glass. There is a line of cypress trees beside it, and the wind has bent them over until they all point inland, like people leaning away from something. Most evenings the fog comes in off the water at about five. After that you cannot see the ocean. You can only hear it.

I arrived at six. She arrived at half past, in her own car, a small green one with a dent in the door. Dinner came from the same restaurant in Half Moon Bay each time, and it was the same dinner. We ate at the long table by the window. She left before seven the next morning. This happened twenty-nine times. It was in my calendar under the word “review.”

Helen talked at that table. She talked more in those evenings than in the twenty-four years before them. She told me about a dog she had as a child that was afraid of its own bowl. She told me she had wanted to be a singer, and that she was exactly good enough to know she wasn’t good enough. Once she got up and lit every candle in the house, nine of them, because she said the place looked like a dentist’s waiting room. I let her. In the morning I put them back in the drawer.
The board would like it to have been a great love, or else a weakness. The public forgives both. It was neither. It was a satisfactory use of a Wednesday.
For Helen it was something else. I could see that it was. She cried on twelve of the twenty-nine occasions. I did not count at the time. I have counted since, for this statement.
On the twentieth Wednesday she asked me a question. We were in the bedroom, in the dark. Somewhere down the coast a foghorn was going, one low note every half minute.
“Do you think about me?” she said. “On the other days?”
I said no.
She was quiet through two notes of the horn.
“You could have lied,” she said.
I said I did not see what a lie would be for.
“No. You wouldn’t.” Then, a little later, she said, “Tell me one thing you’re sorry for. In your whole life. It doesn’t have to be about me. One thing, Ross, and I’ll never ask you again.”
I told her I would have to check.
She laughed at that until she was crying, and then she was only crying, with her back to me. I waited until it stopped. It took some time. Then I slept.
The earring.

On the morning after the twenty-ninth Wednesday I drove her home. She was not able to drive. The fog was still on the coast road, and the ocean below it was the colour of tin. She sat with her head against the window and did not speak. Near Montara my telephone rang. It was a call I had been expecting, about a factory in Ireland. I pulled onto the gravel, got out, and took it. I walked up and down beside the guard rail while I talked. The call went well.
When I got back in, she was sitting up straight and looking through the windscreen.
“Nineteen minutes,” she said.
I said the call had been important.
“I know. I timed it.” She held up her left wrist to show me her watch. Her voice was quite calm. “I wanted to have the number. You like numbers.”

I drove on. She lives in a yellow house in Pacifica with a lemon tree by the step. She got out and walked up the path and left the car door standing open behind her, and I had to lean across the seat and close it myself. She did not come to the coast again. Seven weeks later a newspaper had the calendar, the address of the house, and a photograph of the two of us at the door. Helen had taken it herself on the fourth Wednesday, with her camera propped on the roof of her car. I had thought at the time that she wanted it to keep.

On the morning the newspaper came out, I found the earring. It is gold, a plain small loop. It was in the tray between the seats, where the coins go. She must have taken it off and put it there herself, while I was on the telephone. It had been there for seven weeks, and I had been paying for parking over it. That was five months ago. It is still in the tray.
I am told this is the detail the public wants. I am told to say that it haunts me. It is an earring in a tray. I have not moved it because moving it has not come up.

To the shareholders, to the forty million, and to my wife: I have been advised to say that I am sorry. I am saying it. I understand that you are hurt. I understand it the way I understand that the share price fell. I have seen the number.
That is the statement.

The red lamp stays on. The operator does not say whether it was good. She has not spoken since she arrived. She looks at me over the top of the camera for longer than the crew ever did. Then she switches off the lamp, folds the three legs, and kneels to put the camera in its bag. There is something else in the bag, soft and pale yellow, pushed down at the side. She zips it shut.
I thought it went well.
Somewhere in the house a telephone is ringing.

TAKE 37
The operator hands me a glass of water and the box. I take the tablet. She takes the glass.
It is Thursday. It rained in the night and the canyon is still dripping. I can hear it through the cloth. The lamp is on.

Last Thursday I said that I drove Helen home because she was not able to drive. That was accurate. I did not say why she was not able to drive. Nobody had asked. The operator has not asked either. But the condition is that I say what I did from the beginning, and I began that morning in the middle.
Item two.
There is a song in this one. I will come to it.

The twenty-ninth Wednesday began in the usual way. I arrived at six. The fog was already in, and the cypress trees were dripping onto the roof of the house with a sound like slow fingers on a table. I turned on the lights. I put the food in the oven to keep warm.

Helen arrived at half past. I knew before she was through the door that it would not be a usual evening, because she had not brought her overnight bag. She was carrying a brown cardboard folder, the kind with an elastic band around it. She put it on the long table beside her plate and sat down with her coat still on.
“I’m not staying,” she said. “I want that understood first.”
I said it was understood. I asked whether she wanted to eat.
“No. Sit down, Ross.”
I sat. In daylight you can see the ocean from that table. That night the window was black, and it showed the two of us with the light between us, like people in a painting of a room.
“Did you check?” she said. “You said you’d have to check. That was November.”

I had checked. I told her so. I had gone through the years in order, one at a time, the way I would go through a set of accounts. I told her the answer was no. I said I could name the things other people would expect me to be sorry for, and I offered to list them for her.
“You’d list them.” She pressed the heels of her hands against her eyes. “God. You would actually sit there and read me the list.”
I said I had thought that was what she was asking for.
“I don’t need your list. I’ve kept my own. Twenty-five years.” She took her hands down and laid one on the folder. “It’s in here. The first half of it, anyway. Do you know what this is?”
I said it appeared to be a folder.
She did not laugh. She used to laugh at that kind of answer.

“It’s the notebooks from the valley. Copies. I made them at the time, and I’ve kept them in a shoebox ever since, under my winter sweaters, like a coward.” Her voice was shaking, but she went on. “I’m leaving the company. Friday is my last day. On Monday I’m taking these to the board. And if the board does what I think it will do, which is nothing, I’m taking them to a newspaper.”

By the valley she meant a farm town in the Central Valley of California. The notebooks belong to another Thursday. For now it is enough to say that they record something the company did in that town nineteen years ago. It is true. It would cost the company a great deal.
I did not argue. She was correct on every point and she was within her rights. I told her so.
That is what made her stand up. I have thought about it since, and I believe it was that. If I had shouted, she might have stayed in her chair.
“That’s all?” she said. “I tell you I’m going to burn your house down, and you tell me I’m within my rights?”
I said that she was.
She said my brother’s name then. I am not going to repeat it yet.

“He would have thrown a plate at me,” she said. She was crying now, and angry that she was. “He’d have thrown a plate, and then he’d have helped me carry the box. He was worth ten of you. He’s been in the ground seventeen years, and you have never once said his name in front of me. Not once. I counted that too.”
She picked up the folder and her keys and went out. I went with her. I walk guests to their cars.

The fog was thick on the gravel. The only light was the one over the door, and it made a yellow room in the fog with the two cars standing in it. She opened the driver’s door of the green car and threw the folder across onto the other seat. She did not get in. She stepped back from the open door and turned to face me, with her right hand up on the edge of the roof, her fingers over the frame, where the door shuts.
“Do you know what I think?” she said. “I think there’s nobody in there. I think I’ve been driving out here for a year to talk to a house.”
My telephone began to ring in my jacket.
She heard it. I saw her hear it.
“Go on,” she said. “Answer it. You know you want to.”
She went on talking. I do not remember the words. The telephone went on ringing.
I closed the door. Her hand was in it.

One lawyer has asked me whether I knew her hand was there. He hoped I would say no. I knew where her hand was. I know where things are. I did not close the door in anger. I was not angry. She was talking and the telephone was ringing, and the door was the nearest way to make one of them stop.
It is a heavy door. It broke three of the long bones in the back of her hand. I learned the number later, from the X-ray.

I opened it again at once. She did not scream. I had expected that she would. She made one short sound, like a person who has been pushed into cold water. Then she slid down against the side of the car until she was sitting on the gravel with her hand held against her chest. Her face had gone the colour of the fog.
“Oh,” she said. “Oh, you did. You did.”

I lifted her into the passenger seat of my car. I fastened her seat belt, because she could not. I picked her keys up off the gravel and locked the green car. The telephone had stopped and begun again. I answered it and said that I would call back. The nearest emergency room is thirty-one minutes north. I drove at the speed limit.
The song.

There is no light on that road at night. There was the fog in the headlamps, and the white line, and now and then the eyes of a deer at the edge of a field. Helen was making a noise. It was not crying. It was lower than crying, and it did not stop for breath in the normal places. It was difficult to drive with. So I turned on the radio.

On Wednesday nights a station in San Jose plays old Persian records, and that is where the dial was. A woman was singing. I knew the song before she had finished the first line. My mother used to play it in the kitchen in Shiraz [shee-RAAZ], the city in the south of Iran where I was born. She had a record player with a cracked lid, and she kept it on top of the refrigerator, where the flour could not get into it. She sang along while she rolled out the bread, always half a beat behind the record. I had not heard that song in fifty years. I knew every word.
I sang along. I did not sing loudly. I sang the whole song, beside a woman who was holding her broken hand in her lap. When it ended I waited to hear what they would play next.
At some point Helen had stopped making the noise. She was watching me.
“You’re singing,” she said. It was hardly a voice at all.
I said that I knew the song.
She turned her face to the window. She did not say anything more on that road.
I do not know why I mention the song. The song is not what I did. The door is what I did.
At the hospital there was a nurse at a desk behind glass. She was a big woman with reading glasses on a chain. She looked at Helen’s hand and then at me.
“What happened here?”
“A car door,” I said. That was accurate.
“Whose car door?”
“Hers.”
The nurse looked at Helen. “Honey? Is that right?”
Helen kept her eyes on my face the whole time, as if she were learning it.
“It was a car door,” she said.

They took her through. I sat in the waiting room for two hours and ten minutes. There were orange plastic chairs, a television with the sound off, and a man asleep with a child asleep on top of him. I returned the call. Then a doctor came out and told me they were keeping her until the morning, because the bones had to be set by a surgeon who did not come in at night. Before I left, I went to the desk and asked the nurse whether they stamped tickets for the car park.
She took off her glasses to look at me. Then she stamped it.
The floor of that waiting room had been washed with something that smelled of lemons. I had not thought about that until now.

In the morning I collected her, with her hand in plaster. That is the drive I described last Thursday. Ireland, nineteen minutes, the watch, the earring. I gave it in its correct order. I only left off the front. That afternoon I had her car sent to her on a truck, with the folder still on the seat.

She did not take the notebooks to the board. I do not know why. Seven weeks later she gave a newspaper the calendar, the house and the photograph. She kept the notebooks back, and she kept the door back. The door is the only part I could go to prison for. I have not worked out why she kept it.
To Helen: I am sorry about your hand. I have been advised not to say that on camera, because it admits a crime. I have said it. The operator can cut it.
That is the statement.

The lamp stays on. The operator is not looking at me this time. She is looking at her own right hand, which rests on top of the camera. She turns it over once, slowly, and looks at the back of it. Then she switches off the lamp.
A telephone is ringing. It rings for a long time.

Nepentra does not make you sleepy. You can drive. You can work.
You can look after children.
You will remember everything as well as you did before. Nepentra does not affect your memory.

TAKE 38
The operator hands me a glass of water and the box. I take the tablet. She takes the glass. The water tastes of the glass today. I had not known that glass had a taste.
It is Thursday. The lamp is on.

Item three is older. It is nineteen years old. The board has only ever been told a false account of it, and it is larger than the first two together. Helen called it the valley. I will call it the crossing.
There is a clipboard in this one. I will come to it.
I have to begin with fog, which I did not expect to have to do.

In the Central Valley of California, in the cold months, a fog comes up off the wet ground at night. They call it tule [TOO-lee] fog, after the reeds that grow in the ditches. It is not like the fog on the coast. It does not drift. It sits on the fields as thick as wool, and a man standing at the front of his truck cannot see the back of it. It smells of wet dust and of the fertiliser they put on the cotton. I can smell it now, which is of no use to anyone.

Tres Olmos [trace OL-mose], which is Spanish for Three Elms, is a town of two thousand one hundred people in the south of that valley. It has a school, a church, a gas station, a hall where the farmers hold their meetings, and one railway line. The line runs straight through the fields on a low bank of gravel, and the road to the school goes up over it and down again, like a road going over a sleeping animal. Nineteen years ago that crossing had a sign and no gate. A gate costs four hundred thousand dollars. The railway said the county should pay. The county said the railway should pay. They had been saying it for fourteen years.

On a morning in November a school bus stopped at the sign, as the law requires. The driver had driven that road for twenty-two years. She opened her door to listen, as the law also requires. She heard nothing, because that fog takes sound as well as sight. She drove up onto the line. The train was carrying tomatoes to a cannery.
Nine children died. The youngest was six. The oldest was twelve.

At that time the company had the medicine and did not have permission to sell it. To get permission you must run what is called a trial. You give the medicine to a few hundred people for a year, and you send the government a record of everything that happens to them. We needed a few hundred people. I will be accurate. We needed them to be people the medicine could plainly help.

My brother read about it first. We were in two rooms above a print shop by then, and he came in from the street with the newspaper folded open and put it down on my desk, on top of what I was reading. He did not say anything. He stood with his hand flat on the page, and I saw that he had been crying in the street.
“Nine,” he said. “Look at their faces. Look at that one. She has no front teeth.”
The newspaper had printed their school photographs in three rows of three.
I looked at them. Then I looked at the paragraph underneath, which gave the population of the town.
“How far is it?” I said.
“What?”
“From here. By car.”
He took his hand off the page. He took it away slowly, as if the paper had become hot.
“Why are you asking me that?” he said.
He had not meant what I took him to mean. He had meant, look at this, how terrible. I looked at it and saw a few hundred people.

I want it understood that I believed I was doing good. I still cannot find the step where that stops being true. I drove down two days later. It is four hours, and the last hour is a straight road between cotton fields with nothing on it but telephone poles. Every shop in Tres Olmos was shut. Somebody had tied black ribbon to the pumps at the gas station and to the handle of the church door, and to the elm trees, of which there were only two.

I rented the farmers’ hall. We put in a nurse, a doctor and a coffee urn. We called it a clinic, and it was free. Two hundred and twelve adults came in the first month. All sixteen of the parents came. They sat on folding chairs along the wall with their hands in their laps and waited to be called, and nobody spoke. I had never been in a room so quiet with so many people in it. One woman had a child’s lunch box on her knees, a blue one, and she held it by both ends the whole time she waited. That was Mrs. Aguirre [ah-GEE-reh]. She had lost twin boys. I had not intended to use names.
The clipboard.

By the time the clinic opened, the parents had started a petition, which is a sheet of paper people sign to make a government do something. They wanted the gate. They needed fourteen hundred signatures to force the county to vote on it. The clipboard hung on a nail beside the till in the gas station, between the cigarettes and a rack of maps, with a pen on a string. In the two weeks after the bus, six hundred and eleven people signed. The woman at the till told me they came in with their hats off, as if it were a church.

Here is the difficulty I had. A trial needs a quiet year. The government wants to see the same people, living the same lives, taking the same tablet every week for twelve months. Tres Olmos was not going to be quiet. Lawyers from Los Angeles were already in the motel. They wanted the parents to sue the railway, which means to take it to court for money. Reporters came every week. If the county voted on the gate there would be meetings and marches all winter. My few hundred people would scatter and the year would be wasted.
So I made the town an offer. I will say it plainly, because it is the thing I did.

The company would pay every family in the study forty thousand dollars. For the sixteen parents it would also pay for the funerals and the headstones. In return each adult would sign a paper. The paper said that for the twelve months of the study they would not join a court case, would not speak to reporters, and would not take part in any public campaign. A petition is a public campaign.

I held the meeting myself, on a Friday evening, in the farmers’ hall. I remember that room better than I remember most of the rooms I have lived in. Until this month I could not have told you one thing about it. It smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee. Somebody had already strung Christmas lights along the rafters, and half of them worked. There were two hundred metal folding chairs and every one was taken, and more people stood along the walls, under the framed photographs of prize bulls. Nobody had taken off a coat. A man in the second row kept turning his cap round and round in his hands by the brim.
I stood at the front beside the coffee urn, with the papers in a carton at my feet. My brother sat at a card table with the list of names. I was kind. I meant it.
“I am not from the railway,” I said, “and I am not from the county. I am a chemist. I have brought a doctor and a nurse. They will stay a year, and it will cost you nothing.”
Then I told them about the money. Forty thousand dollars was two years’ wages in the packing sheds, and I watched that number go through the room like wind through a field.
“There is one thing I need in return,” I said. I held up the paper and read it to them.
A woman in a grey cardigan stood up. It was Mrs. Aguirre. Her husband pulled at her sleeve and she took her arm away.
“Forty thousand,” she said. “For what? Say it plain.”
“For a quiet year,” I said.
“Quiet.” She looked round at the others. “He wants us quiet.”
“Rosa,” her husband said.

I turned off the engine. I remember being careful about that. I put on the hand brake so that the car could not roll. The windows were up because of the dust. I shut my door quietly, so as not to wake her.
Then I walked away along the fence towards the oak, because it was cooler there for me, and I answered the call.
“Dr. Bina,” the man in New York said. He had a slow, comfortable voice. “I’ve read your paper twice. Now tell me why I shouldn’t give my money to somebody at Stanford.”
I told him. I talked for a long time.

I want to tell you what I could see, because I was looking at it for all of that time. The whole valley was below me. The bay lay flat and silver, and the salt ponds at the edge of it were red and green, like stained glass laid on the ground. The hills on the far side were the white-gold they go in July, and as the morning came on the heat lifted off them in waves, so that they seemed to be dissolving at the edges, like sugar in a glass. There was a hawk. It hung in one place over the slope for minutes at a time, not moving a feather, held up by nothing but the heat coming off the ground. I watched it while I talked. I remember thinking that I had never seen anything so sure of itself.
The call went well. He asked good questions and I had good answers. I made a joke about my old employers and he laughed, and so did I.
“You know what I like about you?” he said. “You don’t get excited. I’ve had three men on this telephone this week who couldn’t breathe. You sound like a calm man.”
I was not calm. My heart was going like a boy’s. But I was pleased that it did not show.
I walked up and down beside the fence with my free hand in my pocket. My fingers were closed around a very small shoe, and I did not once ask myself what it was.
I was pleased. God help me. I was so pleased.
The call ran fifty-one minutes. I have the telephone record. I have had it for twenty-six years, and for twenty-six years it has been a number.
I should say that the operator is my daughter.

I do not know why I have not said it. She wrote to me in September and asked for the job, and I gave it to her. She is thirty years old. She is standing four steps from me with her hand on the camera. I have told all of it to her face. The woman, and the car door, and the town, and her uncle, and her mother on the kitchen floor. It did not seem to me to need mentioning. Five weeks ago it did not seem to me to weigh anything at all.
I will finish.

When the man in New York had said goodbye, I stood a moment longer under the oak. I was working out how I would tell Shirin. Then I walked back along the fence. The gravel was loud. The car was white in the sun and too bright to look at, and the heat coming off its roof made the air above it shake.
I saw the blanket first. It had slipped down and lay on the floor.
I am not going to tell you what her face looked like. I have the words. I have them in two languages. I find that I will not hand them to a camera.
I broke the window beside her with a stone. The door was not locked. I have never understood why I did that.

I got her out and I knelt on the gravel with her across my knees. She was hot the way a stone is hot. I said her name. I think I said it. A pickup truck stopped on the road, and an old man got down from it with a dog at his heels. He looked once and went back to the truck and came running, as well as he could run, with a plastic jug of water he kept for his radiator.
He poured it over her. He poured it over her head and her chest and her bare foot, and it ran off into the gravel and was gone.
“Come on, sweetheart,” he kept saying. “Come on, now. Come on.”
Then he looked at me. “What’s her name? Mister. What’s her name?”
I could not tell him. I had my mouth open and nothing would come out of it. The dog lay down in the shade of the truck and watched us.
After that there was a fire engine, and a helicopter that landed in the road and blew the dust flat. They took her to the hospital where her mother worked.

Shirin was on the ward when they brought her in. She came down the corridor in her white shoes, half running, with a chart still in her hand, and she saw the stretcher before she saw me. She did not ask me what had happened. She looked at the child, and then she looked at me, and she asked me one thing.
“How long?”
I told her. I had already looked at the telephone.
“Fifty-one minutes,” I said.
She hit me once, with her open hand, in front of the doctors. Then she held on to the front of my shirt with both fists, so that she would not fall.

Our daughter did not die. She lay in that hospital for eleven days without opening her eyes. Shirin sat on one side of the bed and I sat on the other, and we did not speak across it. On the twelfth day our daughter opened her eyes and asked for her blanket.

The doctors said she was a miracle. They said she would be entirely herself. That was true. They did not yet know what else was true, and it is not mine to tell. She is standing here. She can tell it.
Nushin [noo-SHEEN].
I am
I do not seem to be able to
It appears that I am crying. I am told I did at the hospital. I do not remember what that was like, so I cannot say if this is the same.
That is not the statement. I do not have a statement.
The lamp stays on.
WHAT SHE SAID

She comes out from behind the camera. She opens the bag and takes out the soft yellow thing that has been in it since the first Thursday, and she lays it on the table between us. It is smaller than I remembered. It is the colour of butter.
Then she puts her hand into the bag again and takes out a shoe.
It is a child’s left shoe. It is red, with a strap, and the buckle is shaped like a daisy. It would fit in the palm of my hand. She sets it down beside the blanket.
“You can stop now,” she says.
It is the first thing she has said in this room. Her voice is lower than her mother’s. I have not heard it since she was nine. That was the last summer I drove up to Oregon. After it I sent money.

“The small thing first. The tablets are chalk. Chalk and sugar. I pressed them myself in Mom’s garage, with a little machine you can buy for forty dollars. I’ve been putting them in your box since the first Thursday. You’ve taken six of mine. You haven’t had a real one in six weeks.”
I tell her that I worked that out about twenty minutes ago.
“I know. I saw your face when you tasted it.”
She sits down on the floor with her back against the wall, the way her mother used to, and pulls up her knees.

“Now I’m going to say what it does. Nobody ever has. Not you, and not the box.” She looks into the camera when she says it. “Nepentra doesn’t make you forget. You remember every single thing you ever did. It just stops them hurting. That’s the whole medicine.”
Then she looks at me.
“And you made it for me.”
I say yes.
“Tell me if I get this wrong. In most people a hurt wears off. Something terrible happens, and a year later it’s a scar, and they can touch it. The heat burned that out of me. Nothing wears off.

Everything that ever happened to me is still in its first minute. I’m thirty years old and it’s ten to nine on a Thursday in July. The buckle of the car seat is too hot to touch. I can hear you through the glass.”
I say she has not got it wrong.

“So you made a tablet to do for me what I can’t do for myself. Mom told me you sat with me every night for weeks, before she did. Then you went into the kitchen and made it. That’s the best thing I know about you, and I’ve kept it very carefully. You tried it on yourself first, like a good father. It worked on you. And it didn’t work on me, because there’s nothing left in me for it to work on. Forty million people, Dad. And me.”
That is the first time she has called me that since she was nine.
I ask her who told her about the others.

“Helen. She found me in the spring, after her hand. She gave me the notebooks. She told me about the door, and she said she was keeping the door back. She said if you went to prison they’d bring you your tablet every Thursday in a paper cup, and you’d do the years like a man waiting for a bus. She said prison would be wasted on you.”
She is quiet for a moment. Then she says, “Now I want to give you the part you don’t have. You’ve got the outside of that morning. The fence and the hawk. I’ve got the inside. Can I?”
I say she can.

“I woke up because it was quiet. Mister Milk had stopped. I looked out and I could see you by the tree. And I wasn’t scared, Dad. That’s the first thing I need you to know. For a long time I wasn’t scared at all. My shoe was gone, and I thought you had taken it for a walk to cheer it up. You were laughing. I thought, good, it’s working. The shoe said something funny.”
I cannot look at her, and I look at her.

“Then it got hot, and I called you, and you didn’t turn round. And I still wasn’t angry. I was four. I thought you couldn’t hear me because the shoe was talking. I decided to be patient. I remember being proud of how patient I was being. I thought you would tell Mom.”
She presses the back of her hand against her mouth and takes it away again.
“I’m still being patient. That’s what’s wrong with me. It never finished. I never got to the end of waiting for you. I’m in the middle of it right now, while I’m talking to you.”
“Nushin,” I say.

“Let me do the rest. Everybody thinks it’s only the bad things that don’t wear off. It’s everything. I was four, and I loved you the way you love somebody when you’re four. With all of it. That hasn’t worn off either. It can’t. So I can’t hate you. I’ve tried. Mom wanted me to, a little, for my own sake. I haven’t got anywhere to stand to do it from. I’m in the back seat, and I love you, and you’re not turning round. Both of those. For twenty-six years. At full size.”
She reaches up and takes the shoe off the table and holds it in both hands.

“The nurse found this in your jacket at the hospital. Mom kept it. You said you had it in your hand for fifty-one minutes. You had your fingers round it the whole time, and you never asked yourself what it was.”
“No,” I say.

“That’s what the hurt is, Dad. It’s a shoe in your pocket. It’s a small hard thing that doesn’t belong to you. Every time your hand touches it, it asks you two questions. Whose is this? Where is she? That’s all it’s for. It isn’t a punishment. It’s how you find your way back to somebody.”
She turns the shoe over. The sole is hardly worn.

“You thought you could take the hurt out of a person and leave everything else where it was. You can’t. I’d know. It’s one thing. The part of you that hurts over somebody is the same part that holds on to them. So you made a tablet that empties everybody’s pockets. And then Helen was a Wednesday to you. And Mom was a noise in the kitchen. And Uncle Siamak was a signature. And I was a house in Oregon.”
I say that it is accurate. It is the only word I have and I am ashamed of it.
Then I tell her what I have believed for twenty-six years, because it is the last thing I have to put against her.

“A man who keeps from doing harm only because it hurts him afterwards is not a good man,” I say. “He is a dog that has learned where the fence is. A good man would not need the pain. I built a country full of people who do not need it. I thought some of them would turn out to be good anyway.”
“Did they?”
I think about a clipboard on a nail.
“I don’t know,” I say. “I never looked. It didn’t weigh enough to look at.”
She nods slowly.

“Maybe it is a fence,” she says. “I don’t know what good is. I’m the wrong person to ask. I can’t do a wrong thing twice, but that isn’t goodness. That’s just me not being able to put anything down. Maybe there are people who would be kind with empty pockets. I’d like to meet one. But Mom came and sat on my floor every night for years. I asked her once what made her do it. She said, ‘I couldn’t not.’ That was all. She couldn’t not. If that’s a fence, then I think a fence is the best thing people have. I think it might be what holds the roof up.”
Neither of us says anything after that. I do not know which of us is right. I notice that I would like it to be her.
I ask her whether tonight is the punishment, then.

“No. I’m not that kind. I’d have to carry it afterwards. I’ll tell you why I came. I’ve been in that car by myself since I was four. I’m not asking you to get me out. Nobody can. I’m asking you to get in. One night. Sit in the back with me and wait for him to turn round. It has to be you. You’re the only other person who was there.”
I ask what happens after the one night.

“Nothing. I’ve got a real one in my pocket. I’ll put it on the table in the morning. You can take it and go back to being the calm man. I won’t stop you. I’ll go on being patient. I don’t get a choice about that.”
She holds out the shoe.
“Put it in your pocket.”
I take it. It weighs almost nothing. I put it in the pocket of my jacket, on the left side, where it was before. I can feel it through the cloth.
“It’ll be tonight,” she says. “The last of the real ones is leaving you. I’ll be in the chair.”
THE NIGHT
I wake on the floor of the long room and it is hot.

The grey cloth over the window is lit from behind, and it is not a cloth. It is the silver screen people put inside a car to keep the sun off the seats. The light comes through its edges white. A telephone is ringing somewhere outside. I think, I should get up and answer that, and I cannot get up, because there is a strap across my chest.
I wake.

I am standing on gravel in the dark above the ocean, and my hand is up on the cold edge of a car roof, with my fingers over the frame, where the door shuts. A man is standing beside me. He is calm. He is listening to a telephone ring in his jacket. I know what he is going to do, because I have always known where things are, and I say to him, my hand is there, you can see my hand is there. He closes the door.

It is not as I described it. I said three bones. I gave it a number. It does not have a number. It is the whole of the world arriving in one place, and under it, worse than it, is the face of a man who is waiting to see what the radio will play next.
I wake.

Fog. I am at the till of a gas station, and there is a clipboard on a nail, and the pen is swinging on its string as if someone has just let it go. Behind me in the fog there are children talking, a whole bus of them, quite close, and a woman’s voice saying sit down, sit down now, we’re nearly there. I pick up the pen. I want to sign. I want it more than I have wanted anything. The girl at the till looks at me kindly and says, you’re not a resident. From down the road my brother says, “All right.” The whole message takes eleven seconds. I listen to all eleven. I had only ever counted them.
I wake.

A kitchen, and aeroplanes going over like beads on a string, and somebody is on the floor with their back against the stove, making a sound. I look for her. There is nobody on the floor but me. The sound is coming out of my own mouth. It is the whole winter. It is every night somebody did not go down the hall. A telephone is ringing on the wall, and a man steps over me to answer it, and I look up as he passes and he does not look down.
I wake, and I am small.

My feet do not reach the floor. One of them has no shoe on. There is a strap over each shoulder and a buckle on my chest that is too hot to touch, and I touch it anyway, again and again, because I have seen it opened and I cannot remember how. The air is thick and tastes of plastic. The blanket has slid off my knees and I cannot reach it. I want it more than I want to breathe.
Through the glass there is a wire fence and one oak tree and a man in a grey jacket.

He is walking up and down. He has one hand in his pocket. He is looking out at a valley, at a hawk, at hills that are dissolving like sugar, and he is laughing. I can hear him through the glass. I call him. I call him by the only name I have for him. He is so pleased. He does not turn round.

It is fifty-one minutes. I had the record for twenty-six years and I did not know what was on it. It is not a number. It is one minute, and then it is another minute exactly as long, and then another, and in every one of them he could turn round and he does not. I am in all of them. I do not get to skip any.

And somewhere in the middle of it, in the heat, a hand closes over mine on the buckle. It is a grown hand, a woman’s, not quite steady. She does not open the buckle. She cannot. She only keeps her hand there over mine.
She has been here the whole time. She has been here since ten to nine. She was four and then she was nine and then she was thirty, and it was always this minute, and nobody came.

It is very crowded in the car. Helen is here, holding her hand. The ten children are here, and Mr. Aguirre, and my brother with his glasses pushed up, and Shirin with a blue cup in both hands. Everyone I ever hurt is in this car. And still it is only the two of us, a child and a child, with the windows up, waiting for a man to turn round.
I stop calling him. I hold her hand.
That is all I do, all night. It is the first thing I have done for her in twenty-one years.
THE MORNING
It is light. The cloth over the window is a cloth.

I am on the floor of the long room with my back against the wall. Every part of me aches, as if I had been carried a long way and set down badly. My daughter is asleep in the chair with her knees drawn up. I had not known that she could sleep. Her hand is hanging down over the arm of the chair, and it is six inches from mine.
Through the open door and the kitchen window beyond it, I can see the persimmon tree from where I am sitting. The sun is in it. Every fruit is lit.

It is all still here. I had thought the morning might take some of it away, the way mornings do. It has not. Helen’s hand is here. The clipboard is here. The eleven seconds are here, and the blue cup, and fifty-one minutes, each one as long as it was. I know now what they weigh. I could not have told you yesterday. I can tell you to the ounce.

I understand, sitting here, that there are things I have to do. I can list them. There is a woman in a town in the valley who lost two sons, then a husband and a daughter, and who was told it was my brother’s doing. There is a board. There is a government. There is a house in Oregon with a view of a river. I have never in my life felt so clearly what I ought to do. And I know why I feel it. I feel it because it hurts. I was right about that for twenty-six years. A man does the right thing because the wrong thing will not leave him alone. Being right about it does not help me at all.
On the table there is the yellow blanket.

Beside the blanket there is a glass of water and a white box with a blue band. The box is open. There is one tablet in it. It has a line scored across the middle. I do not need to taste it to know that this one is real.
She has left the camera on. The red lamp is lit.
Nushin stirs in the chair. She does not open her eyes. She says, “It’s Friday, Dad. You never took it on a Friday.”
I look at the tablet. I look at my daughter’s hand.
My own hand is in my jacket pocket. There is a small hard thing in it that does not belong to me.
The lamp is on.
THE STATEMENT

The board had asked for every Thursday’s recording, and it had all six. On the following Monday the company released a statement by its founder. It had been recorded nearly six weeks earlier, and the board had cut it to four minutes.
It was Take 36.
Commentators called it measured. One called it dignified. A man on a business programme said that it was a relief, frankly, to see somebody keep his head.
By Thursday the share price had recovered the whole eleven per cent.
A teacher in Fresno got her four thousand dollars back before she was out of bed. She took her tablet with a glass of water and went to work.

GLOSSARY
Aguirre [ah-GEE-reh] — A Spanish family name.
Bina [bee-NAA] — Persian, one who sees. A family name.
Nepentra [neh-PEN-tra] — From the Greek, no grief. The medicine
Rostam makes. In the old Greek poem the Odyssey, Helen stirs a drug called nepenthes [neh-PEN-theez] into the wine so that the men at her table can hear about their dead without weeping.
Nepentrine [neh-PEN-treen] — The chemical name printed in small letters on the box.
Nushin [noo-SHEEN] — Persian, the sweet one. A woman’s name.
Inside it is nush, the first half of nushdaru [noosh-da-ROO], the healing balm of the old Persian stories.

Rostam [ROS-tam] — A Persian man’s name. In the Persian Book of Kings, Rostam is the greatest of the heroes. He wounds his own child in battle without knowing who it is, and sends for the healing balm. It comes too late.
Shiraz [shee-RAAZ] — A city in the south of Iran.
Shirin [shee-REEN] — Persian, sweet. A woman’s name.
Siamak [see-yaa-MAK] — A Persian man’s name.
Tres Olmos [trace OL-mose] — Spanish, three elms. An invented farm town in the Central Valley of California.
Tule [TOO-lee] — A reed that grows in the ditches of the Central
Valley. Tule fog is the thick ground fog named for it.
